mainTopic: The laws learned from ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ and ״בעל השור נקי״: the bans on a slaughtered שור הנסקל and its hide, and רבי אליעזר's exemption from half the כופר.
overview: The גמרא finishes defending רבי אבהו's view that ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ forbids a שור הנסקל even if it was properly slaughtered. It rejects the idea that this applies only to slaughter with a flint, because a flint is as valid as a knife for שחיטה. Then it explains that ״בעל השור נקי״ adds a ban on benefit from the hide. תנאים who use that phrase for something else learn the hide ban from the extra word ״אֶת״ in ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״. The תנא who does not learn from ״אֶת״ is backed by the story of שמעון העמסוני, who stopped expounding ״אֶת״ until רבי עקיבא explained it. Next, רבי אליעזר reads ״בעל השור נקי״ as freeing the owner of a שור תם from half the כופר. When רבי עקיבא says this is obvious, רבי אליעזר answers with cases where the ox is not stoned: proof by one witness or by the owner's admission (since כופר is כפרה, not קנס), or an ox that meant to kill something else. The amud ends as רב כהנא and רב טביומי argue which answer came first, and a fisherman משל that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Maybe the ban applies only when he slaughtered with a flint
steps.stepSummary: A suggestion that ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ forbids the slaughtered ox only when it was slaughtered with a stone, because that resembles סקילה. A knife-slaughtered ox would then be allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe the Torah forbade it only where he checked a flint stone and slaughtered with it, since that is a kind of stoning. But where he slaughtered it with a knife, it would not be forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a challenge to רבי אבהו. Maybe the verse forbids the ox only in the narrow case where it was slaughtered with a stone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו learned from ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ that even a properly slaughtered שור הנסקל is forbidden. This challenge tries to shrink that rule: maybe a stone slaughter is forbidden only because it looks like סקילה. If so, an ox slaughtered with a knife would be permitted, and the verse would teach much less.

keyTerms.meaning: A flint stone with a sharp edge
Stoning (the death the Torah gives a killer ox)

phrases.english: Where he checked a flint
and slaughtered with it,
since he did to it something like stoning,
but where he slaughtered it with a knife – not!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge to רבי אבהו from the previous part of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's claim that ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ forbids any slaughtered שור הנסקל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse might refer only to slaughter with a stone, which looks like stoning. So it does not prove that every kind of slaughter is forbidden.

steps.title: The Torah never requires a knife, and a flint is valid
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is rejected. Nothing in the Torah makes a knife special, and a משנה rules that slaughtering with a sickle, a flint, or a reed is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: Is a knife written in the Torah? But we learned in a משנה: One who slaughters with a hand-sickle, a flint, or a reed, his slaughter is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the flint-versus-knife split. A flint is a perfectly kosher tool for שחיטה, just like a knife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion needed a knife to be the 'real' slaughtering tool, so that a flint would look different and stone-like. But the Torah never mentions a knife, and the משנה treats flint, sickle and reed as fully valid. A flint slaughter is a normal שחיטה, so the verse cannot be limited to it, and רבי אבהו's broad reading stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (a doubtful question)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this משנה permits sloppy slaughter. It means any tool with a smooth, sharp edge works, so a knife has no special status in the Torah.

phrases.english: They said: Is a knife written in the Torah?
But didn't we learn: One who slaughters with a hand-sickle,
with a flint, or with a reed –
his slaughter is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the limitation suggested in step 1.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It wrongly assumes a knife is the Torah's standard tool. In fact a flint is an equally valid tool for שחיטה, as the משנה shows.

steps.title: Then why do we need 'the owner of the ox shall be clear'?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו learns both the eating ban and the benefit ban from ״לא יאכל את בשרו״. So what is left for the phrase ״בעל השור נקי״ to teach?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that he learns both the ban on eating and the ban on benefit from 'its flesh shall not be eaten,' why do I need 'the owner of the ox shall be clear'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the extra phrase ״בעל השור נקי״ adds in רבי אבהו's view. It seems to have nothing left to teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not waste words. If one phrase already covers both אכילה and הנאה, the second phrase looks extra. The גמרא wants to find a separate job for ״בעל השור נקי״.

keyTerms.meaning: And now (that we have said this)
He derives it, he learns it
A ban on getting any benefit from something

phrases.english: And now that he derives
the ban on eating and the ban on benefit
from 'its flesh shall not be eaten,'
why do I need 'the owner of the ox shall be clear'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשְׁתָּא דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ אִיסּוּר אֲכִילָה וְאִיסּוּר הֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רבי אבהו's reading is secured, the גמרא asks what the second phrase is for.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra law ״בעל השור נקי״ teaches according to רבי אבהו

steps.title: It teaches that benefit from the hide is also forbidden
steps.stepSummary: ״בעל השור נקי״ teaches that even the hide is forbidden for benefit. Otherwise we might have thought only the flesh is forbidden, since the verse says 'its flesh.'
steps.simpleTranslation: For benefit from its hide. You might have thought: only its flesh is forbidden for benefit, but its hide would be permitted for benefit. So it teaches us 'the owner of the ox shall be clear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ״בעל השור נקי״ extends the benefit ban to the hide of the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ says 'its flesh,' so it could be read as covering only the meat. ״בעל השור נקי״ means the owner is left 'clean' of the whole ox and gets no benefit from any part of it, including the hide.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have thought to say

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי אבהו: ״לא יאכל את בשרו״ forbids eating and benefit from the meat of a slaughtered שור הנסקל, and ״בעל השור נקי״ adds that the hide is forbidden too.

phrases.english: For benefit from its hide.
For it could enter your mind to say:
it is its flesh that is forbidden for benefit,
but its hide will be permitted for benefit;
so it teaches us 'the owner of the ox shall be clear.'

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״בעל השור נקי״ forbids benefit from the hide, which the word 'its flesh' alone might not include.

steps.title: Where do the other תנאים learn that the hide is forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: Some תנאים use ״בעל השור נקי״ for a different teaching, which the גמרא will bring later. So what is their source for the ban on benefit from the hide?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for those תנאים who take 'the owner of the ox shall be clear' for another teaching, as we will say below, where do they learn the ban on benefit from its hide?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. If some תנאים use ״בעל השור נקי״ for something else, where do they get the hide ban?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 gave ״בעל השור נקי״ the job of forbidding the hide. But other תנאים already use that phrase for a different lesson, so it is not free for them to teach about the hide. The גמרא now has to find another source for the hide ban in their view.

keyTerms.meaning: תנאים, the sages of the משנה era
Who take it out (use the verse) for
Another teaching learned from a verse
From where do they know it?

phrases.english: And according to those תנאים
who take this 'the owner of the ox shall be clear'
for another teaching
[as we will want to say below],
phrases.notes: Some versions add the words in square brackets. They point ahead to רבי אליעזר's teaching a little later on this amud.

phrases.english: from where do they learn the ban on benefit from its hide?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְהָנָךְ תַּנָּאֵי דְּמַפְּקִי לֵיהּ לְהַאי בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי לִדְרָשָׁה אַחֲרִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 4's use of ״בעל השור נקי״ for the hide and asks about תנאים who use the phrase differently.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the ban on benefit from the hide, according to תנאים who use ״בעל השור נקי״ for another teaching

steps.title: The hide ban comes from the extra word ״אֶת״
steps.stepSummary: Those תנאים learn the hide ban from the word ״אֶת״ in ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״, which adds something attached to the flesh: the hide.
steps.simpleTranslation: They learn it from ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״: ״אֶת״ means whatever is attached to its flesh. What is that? Its hide.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 5's question. The extra word ״אֶת״ in the פסוק teaches that the hide is forbidden too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said just ״בְּשָׂרוֹ״, 'its flesh.' The extra ״אֶת״ widens the ban to something that goes along with the flesh, and that is the hide. So these תנאים don't need ״בעל השור נקי״ for the hide, and they can use it for their other teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: A small Hebrew word in a פסוק that some read as adding something extra
Something attached or secondary to the main thing

phrases.english: They derive it from "et besaro" (its flesh) –
phrases.notes: The פסוק is ״וְלֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״ (שמות 21:28). The focus is on the extra word ״אֶת״.

phrases.english: "et" adds what is secondary to its flesh,
what is that? Its hide.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra word ״אֶת״ in ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״ adds the hide to the ban.

steps.title: The other opinion does not learn from ״אֶת״
steps.stepSummary: The תנא who learns the hide ban from ״בעל השור נקי״ does not learn laws from the word ״אֶת״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this תנא does not expound the word ״אֶת״.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the other opinion needed ״בעל השור נקי״ for the hide. That תנא simply does not learn laws from ״אֶת״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Otherwise we would ask: why didn't that תנא just use ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״ like the others? The answer is that, for him, ״אֶת״ is just a normal grammar word and teaches nothing. So he had to find another source for the hide.

keyTerms.meaning: A sage from the time of the משנה
Does not expound (does not learn a law from it)

phrases.english: And this tanna –
phrases.notes: He means the תנא from Step 4, who learns the hide ban from ״בעל השור נקי״.

phrases.english: does not expound "et".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the opinion from Step 4 could not use the source given in Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא who uses ״בעל השור נקי״ for the hide does not learn laws from the word ״אֶת״.

steps.title: The story of שמעון העמסוני who stopped expounding ״אֶת״
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells that שמעון העמסוני expounded every ״אֶת״ in the תורה, but stopped at ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״. He said he was rewarded for stopping just as for expounding.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: שמעון העמסוני, and some say נחמיה העמסוני, used to expound every ״אֶת״ in the תורה. When he reached ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״, he stopped. His students asked: רבי, what happens to all the ״אֶתִּין״ you already expounded? He told them: Just as I got reward for expounding, I get reward for stopping.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show there really is a view that does not learn laws from ״אֶת״. A great sage gave up this method entirely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמעון העמסוני learned something extra from every ״אֶת״. But at the פסוק about fearing ה׳, he could not think of anything that should be feared alongside ה׳. So he dropped the whole method, and his earlier teachings from ״אֶת״ fell with it.

keyTerms.meaning: The many times the word ״אֶת״ appears

steps.confusionAlert: פֵּירַשׁ here does not mean 'he explained.' It means 'he withdrew' or 'he stopped.'

phrases.english: As it is taught: Shimon HaAmasoni,
and some say Neḥemya HaAmasoni,
would expound every "et" in the Torah.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״, פֵּירַשׁ.
phrases.english: Once he reached "You shall fear the Lord your God," he withdrew.
phrases.notes: דברים 6:13. He couldn't think of anything to fear alongside ה׳, so he stopped.

phrases.english: His students said to him:
Our teacher, all the "et"s that you expounded –
what will become of them?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁקִּבַּלְתִּי שָׂכָר עַל הַדְּרִישָׁה,
phrases.english: He said to them: Just as I received reward for the expounding,
so I received reward for the withdrawing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for Step 7's claim that some do not expound ״אֶת״.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that there is a view that does not learn laws from ״אֶת״.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about שמעון העמסוני, who gave up expounding ״אֶת״.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: ״אֶת״ includes תלמידי חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא taught that the ״אֶת״ in ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״ includes fearing תלמידי חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until רבי עקיבא came and taught: ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״ — this includes תלמידי חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by showing that רבי עקיבא did find a meaning for this ״אֶת״. We must also fear and respect Torah scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem that stopped שמעון העמסוני was that nothing seemed fit to be feared alongside ה׳. רבי עקיבא answered that תלמידי חכמים are. Still, the point for our sugya stands: some תנאים do not learn from ״אֶת״, which is why one opinion needed ״בעל השור נקי״ for the hide.
steps.whatToRemember: The ban on the hide of a stoned ox comes either from ״אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ״ (for those who expound ״אֶת״) or from ״בעל השור נקי״ (for those who don't). רבי עקיבא expounds ״אֶת״, even in ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״.

phrases.english: Until Rabbi Akiva came and taught:
"You shall fear the Lord your God" –
to include Torah scholars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ברייתא from Step 8 by giving a meaning for the ״אֶת״ that had stopped שמעון העמסוני.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ״אֶת״ in ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״ includes fearing תלמידי חכמים.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: The owner is free from half the ransom
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that רבי אליעזר learns from ״וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי״ that the owner of a שור תם that killed a person does not pay half the כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: "But the owner of the ox shall be clear." רבי אליעזר says: he is clear from paying half a ransom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the other teaching from ״וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי״ that it mentioned in step 5. According to רבי אליעזר, the פסוק frees the owner of a שור תם from paying half the כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שור תם that damages property pays half the damage. So you might think that a שור תם that kills a person makes its owner pay half the כופר. רבי אליעזר says the פסוק rules that out, which means he does not use these words for the ban on benefiting from the hide.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money the owner pays when his ox kills a person
Half the ransom, like the half damages a שור תם pays

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the reason some תנאים cannot use ״וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי״ for the hide ban (steps 5–6).

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"But the owner of the ox shall be clear"
Rabbi Eliezer says:
he is clear from half a ransom.
phrases.notes: This is about a שור תם, an ox with no history of goring, which normally pays half.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי״ – רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fulfills the promise of step 5 by bringing the alternative reading of ״וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי״.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר, the owner of a שור תם that killed a person is exempt from half the כופר.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: That is obvious, since a תם pays only from its own body
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא challenges that no פסוק is needed. A שור תם pays only from its own body, and this ox is being stoned, so there is nothing to collect from.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: But isn't the damage of a תם itself paid only from the ox's body? The owner can say, "Bring it to court and it will pay you!"
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא attacks רבי אליעזר's reading and says the פסוק would be teaching something we already know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Half damages of a שור תם are collected only from the ox itself. The owner can simply hand the ox over. An ox that killed a person is stoned and worth nothing, so of course the owner pays nothing, and the פסוק would be unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: From its body; payment taken only from the value of the ox itself
Bring it to court; the owner hands over the ox instead of paying from his own money
But isn't it so...; opens a challenge

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
But isn't it itself
phrases.notes: He means the ordinary half damages of a שור תם.

phrases.english: paid only from its body?
"Bring it to court and it will pay you!"

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: וַהֲלֹא הוּא עַצְמוֹ אֵין מִשְׁתַּלֵּם אֶלָּא מִגּוּפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אליעזר's reading in step 10 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's claim that the פסוק exempts the owner from half the כופר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A שור תם pays only from its own body. A stoned ox has no value, so the exemption follows by logic and the פסוק would be pointless.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: The ox was not put to death
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר answers that he is not talking about an ox that gets stoned. He means a killing proven only by one witness or by the owner's admission, where the ox stays alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said to him: Is that how I look in your eyes, that my teaching is about an ox that is put to death? My teaching is only about a case where it killed a person and this is known through one witness or through the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר defends his reading by narrowing the case to one where the ox is not killed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One witness or the owner's admission is not enough to stone the ox, so the ox remains alive and has value to pay from. You might think half the כופר could be collected from it, so the פסוק is needed to say the owner is clear.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that how I look in your eyes? Do you think I would say something so obvious?
Liable to death, meaning the ox is stoned
A single witness, not enough to put the ox to death
Based on the owner's own admission

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said to him:
Is that how I am in your eyes,
that my ruling is about this one that is liable to death?
My ruling is only
where it killed a person
based on one witness,
or based on the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: כָּךְ אֲנִי בְּעֵינֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי עקיבא's challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא understood the case as an ox that is stoned, where there is nothing to pay from.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is an ox that stays alive because the proof is weak, and the פסוק teaches that no half כופר is paid even from it.

steps.title: The owner's admission already exempts him from a fine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the case of the owner's admission. Someone who admits to a קנס does not pay it, so no פסוק is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Based on the owner?! He is admitting to a fine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges one half of רבי אליעזר's answer, the case of the owner's admission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this view the כופר counts as a קנס, and a person who admits to a קנס is exempt. So when the owner admits, the exemption is already known without the פסוק, and the problem of an unnecessary פסוק comes back for that case.

keyTerms.meaning: Admits to an act that brings a fine; he is exempt from paying it
A fine, a set penalty and not repayment of an actual loss

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is only against the owner's admission. The case of one witness is not attacked here.

phrases.english: Based on the owner?!
He is admitting to a fine!

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל פִּי בְעָלִים?! מוֹדֶה בִּקְנָס הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second case in רבי אליעזר's answer in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of the owner's admission in רבי אליעזר's answer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who admits to a קנס is exempt anyway, so the פסוק would teach nothing new in that case.

steps.title: Ransom is atonement, not a fine
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר holds that כופר is a כפרה, not a קנס, so an owner who admits would normally have to pay it. That is why the פסוק is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that ransom is atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 13. It explains that רבי אליעזר does not see כופר as a קנס at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed כופר is a קנס, and a person who admits to a קנס does not pay. But if כופר is a כפרה, an owner who admits should pay it to atone. So without the פסוק we would make him pay, and the פסוק is needed to free him.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money paid when an ox kills a person

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up כופר and קנס. The whole answer depends on saying כופר is atonement, not a fine, so the rule 'admitting to a קנס does not obligate payment' does not apply.

phrases.english: He holds that ransom is atonement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13 about the owner's admission.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the nature of the payment (כפרה rather than קנס)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כופר is a קנס, so an admitting owner would not pay anyway, and no פסוק is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: כופר is a כפרה, so an admitting owner would pay, and the פסוק is needed to free him in the case of a שור תם.

steps.title: Another answer: the ox meant to kill something else
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא records a different reply from רבי אליעזר. His case is an ox that meant to kill an animal, a non-Jew, or a non-viable baby, but killed a viable Jewish person instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר said to him, 'עקיבא, is this how I look in your eyes, that my ruling is about an ox that must be put to death? My ruling is only about an ox that meant to kill an animal and killed a person, meant to kill a non-Jew and killed a Jew, or meant to kill non-viable babies and killed a viable person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different ברייתא with a second answer to רבי עקיבא's challenge from step 11. It gives a new case where the ox is not stoned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox is only stoned if it meant to kill the person it killed. If it aimed at something it is not stoned for and hit a person by mistake, it stays alive. Then there is something to collect from, so the פסוק is needed to free the owner of a שור תם from half the כופר.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a second, separate way to explain רבי אליעזר. It sets up the next question: which of the two answers did he say first?

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
Rabbi Eliezer said to him: Akiva,
is this how I appear in your eyes,
that my ruling is about this one, which must be put to death?
My ruling is only where it intended

phrases.aramaic: לַהֲרוֹג אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וְהָרַג אֶת הָאָדָם;
phrases.english: to kill the animal, and it killed the person;
to kill a non-Jew, and it killed a Jew;
to kill non-viable babies, and it killed a viable person.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ, אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: עֲקִיבָא, כָּךְ אֲנִי בְּעֵינֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to רבי עקיבא's challenge, different from the answer in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so the ox is not stoned
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אליעזר is talking about an ox that gets stoned, so there is nothing to collect from.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is talking about an ox that meant to kill something else and is not stoned, so the פסוק is needed.

steps.title: Which answer came first?
steps.stepSummary: Since the two ברייתות give two different answers, the גמרא asks which one רבי אליעזר said first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one did he say to him first?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about order. This sets up the two opinions that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both answers are accepted as coming from רבי אליעזר. The question is only which one he said first, and the next step brings two views.

phrases.english: Which one did he say to him first?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the answer in step 12 with the answer in step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The order in which רבי אליעזר gave his two answers.

steps.title: Two views in the name of רבא
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא says in the name of רבא that the 'intending' answer came first. רב טביומי says in the name of רבא that the 'killed' answer came first.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רבא: he said 'intending' to him first. רב טביומי said in the name of רבא: he said 'killed' to him first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with two opinions that both quote רבא but disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Intending' is the answer from step 15, about the ox that aimed at something else. 'Killed' is the answer from step 12, about one witness or the owner's admission. They argue about which came first.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said in the name of Rava:
He said 'intending' to him first.
phrases.notes: This is the answer from step 15, the ox that meant to kill something else.

phrases.english: Rav Tavyumei said in the name of Rava:
He said 'killed' to him first.
phrases.notes: This is the answer from step 12: one witness or the owner's admission.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב כהנא: the 'intending' answer came first. רב טביומי: the 'killed' answer came first.

steps.title: רב כהנא's view explained with a fisherman
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins explaining why רב כהנא says the 'intending' answer came first, using a משל of a fisherman pulling fish from the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רבא that he said 'intending' to him first. It is like a fisherman pulling fish out of the sea,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב כהנא's view so it can explain the reason behind it. It starts a משל, and the rest continues in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא repeats the words on purpose, this time to give a reason, not just the opinion. The reason is told through a משל of a fisherman. The full meaning only becomes clear when the משל is finished.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said in the name of Rava
that he said 'intending' to him first:

phrases.aramaic: מָשָׁל לְצַיָּד שֶׁשּׁוֹלֶה דָּגִים מִן הַיָּם,
phrases.english: it is like a fisherman pulling fish out of the sea,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר ״מִתְכַּוֵּון״ אֲמַר לֵיהּ בְּרֵישָׁא מָשָׁל לְצַיָּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats רב כהנא's opinion from step 17 in order to explain its reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב כהנא's view that the 'intending' answer came first is explained through a משל of a fisherman, which continues in the next part of the daf.
